Shane Gillis hopped on Joe Rogan’s podcast to address his controversial Saturday Night Live monologue last month.

During his mediocre stint on the stage, during which he name drops Rogan’s sauna, the comedian said that women who wear workout clothes at the gym were “dressing like whores.” When recalling the controversy with Rogan, Gillis said that the NBC sketch comedy show didn’t remove the joke from his monologue because they don’t review it before it goes on air. “Not to defend SNL, they don’t approve it. I’m sure non-comics, they write the set for them. They have writers that write the monologue for them.”

Notably, most non-comedians have their monologues penned by the staff, with Taylor Swift (who memorably wrote her monologue song in 2009) being the exception. And while SNL did inquire about Gillis’ monologue, he promised them there would be nothing to fuss over. “The funniest part was, they were like, ‘What’s going on with the monologue?’ And I was like, ‘It’s not great but I don’t say anything bad,'” he said. “The whole time, I was like, ‘Fellas, I’m giving you a solid C minus of a monologue but I promise there’s no controversy. I’m calling myself fat for fucking 10 minutes. That’s it.'”

Gillis was fired from SNL in 2019 for racist and homophobic comments, but has been invited back to host three times since. During his recent appearance, he not only infuriated viewers but dropped a F-bomb during one of the sketches, a Dr. Seuss-themed bit titled “Green Eggs and Ham.”

#3324. Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler Is 2027 IEEE President-Elect

He has been an active volunteer for more than 30 years

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler is the 2027 IEEE president-elect.

IEEE Life Fellow Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler has been elected as the 2027 IEEE president-elect. He will begin serving as president on 1 January 2028.

Schindler, who was nominated by the IEEE Board of Directors, received 16,421 votes in the election. Senior Member David Alan Koehler received 13,874 votes.

Schindler’s Top 3 Goals as President-Elect Strengthen IEEE’s connection with industry by coordinating events across geography, industry, and technology to revitalize professional activities, especially ones for young professionals.Champion the improvement of IEEE’s digital infrastructure to eliminate manual processes and modernize interfaces.Prioritize the advancement of technology to benefit future generations by expanding and supporting IEEE initiatives and programs.

At press time, the results were unofficial until the IEEE Board of Directors accepts the IEEE Teller’s Committee report in November.

Schindler, an expert in microwave semiconductor technology, is an independent consultant supporting clients with technical expertise, due diligence, and project management.

Throughout his career, he led the development of microwave integrated-circuit technology, from lab demonstrations to high-volume commercial products. He has numerous technical publications and holds 11 patents.

Schindler served as CTO of Anlotek, and director of Qorvo and RFMD’s Boston design center. He was applications manager at IBM, engineering manager at ATN Microwave, and a lab manager at Raytheon.

An IEEE volunteer for more than 30 years, Schindler served as the 2024 vice president of IEEE Technical Activities and the 2021–2022 Division IV director. He was chair of the IEEE Conferences Committee from 2015 to 2018 and president of the IEEE Microwave Theory and Technology Society (MTTS) in 2003. He received the society’s 2018 Distinguished Service Award and its 2015 N. Walter Cox Award. His award-winning micro-business column has appeared in IEEE Microwave Magazine since 2011.

He also led the 2025 One IEEE to Enable Strategic Investments in Innovations and Public Imperative Activities adhoc committee.

Schindler is an IEEE–Eta Kappa Nu member and a MTTS honorary life member.

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3323. Lifehacker's Pick for the Best TV to Gift in 2026 Isn't Actually a TV

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

#3322. watchOS 27.3: Three new features coming soon to Apple Watch

watchOS 27.3 will launch to all users next month and introduce these three new Apple Watch features.

Siri AI keeps getting new features and also expanding to more languages. And in watchOS 27.3, the assistant will improve in both categories.

watchOS 27.3 upgrades Siri AI with new app actions across built-in apps like Calendar, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, and Weather. With these capabilities, Siri on your wrist can do more than ever.

There are also four new Siri AI languages supported in watchOS 27.3: Chinese (traditional), Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

For the latest Apple Watch models, watchOS 27.3 adds a new Audio Intelligence feature called Live Rewind. Per Apple’s website:

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

I’m curious to see how useful this proves in everyday life. When Apple demoed the feature in September, it showed Live Rewind being used at a restaurant when an Apple Watch user missed part of the server’s menu explanation. Asking the server to repeat what they said seems like an easier solution, but perhaps there are other occasions Live Rewind will come in handy.

It won’t be for everyone, but I’ve been testing watchOS 27.3’s new Siri Recap feature and really love it.

Siri Recap only works on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and it’s off by default. But if you have one of those models and enable the feature, Siri can create automatic logs of what’s happening in your day-to-day life.

Most of the time, you won’t need to reference any of the recaps and they’ll be automatically deleted after a week. But based on my experience with the feature, Siri Recap definitely comes in handy at times when trying to remember key details from conversations.

#3320. Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill

Congress needs accurate technical insights

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum.

During this year’s Congressional Visits Day, Nikhil Jathar [second from left] and three other IEEE members met with Nile Whitmore [middle], a legislative assistant for Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas).

When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.

“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”

What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.

Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:

Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”

For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits.

Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.

On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”

Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”

For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.

A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.

“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology

The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?

During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls.

Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.

“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.

It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.

And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”

Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum. He covers how emerging technologies are changing the balance of power between companies, governments, and individuals. The rest of the time, he worries about his own balance on a bicycle, skis, or the side of a mountain.

I found it difficult to get answers from legislative offices, so I'd love to hear what's missing in this story from any legislative staffers either here in the comments or at my email address (on our About page). I also know that things work somewhat differently in each country--are there readers in India or Germany or Chile who might be able to share their experiences working with lawmakers there?

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. I’ve been testing the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX boots for the last month on all of my hikes, and they’ve proved to be some of the best hiking boots for any season and any terrain. They look the part too, which helps me feel unstoppable on the trail.

Mocha/Redwood, Cypress/Azalea, Carbon/Redwood, Gravel/Cypress

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are available to purchase on the La Sportiva website for $249 in the U.S. and £220 in the U.K. The color selection differs between territories. In the U.S., there are only two choices — Carbon/Redwood or Mocha/Redwood — and in the U.K. you can choose from Cypress/Azalea, Carbon/Redwood or Gravel/Cypress. You can also purchase the shoes on Amazon for $310 in the U.S., but sizes and colors are limited.

When deciding on the boot size, you will need to convert from European sizing, since this is how the boots are sold on the site. The boots are available in women’s EUR sizes 36 to 42.5 with half sizes, and men’s EUR sizes 40 to 48.5 with half sizes. I’m usually a U.K. size 5 and needed to size up since the boots have a very snug fit. I ended up purchasing an EUR size 39, which is a U.K. size 6 and a U.S. women’s size 7.5.

These boots are certainly on the more expensive side, but it’s not hard to see why. They’re very well made and comfortable to walk in. Also very supportive are the Scarpa Cyrus 2 Mid GTX. These boots cost $240, but this is the price to pay for a boot you’d happily spend your life walking in.

Another boot with excellent ankle support is the Keen Targhee IV, which costs $169. They’ve been my go-to boots for taking on the outdoors for over a year now, but I think the La Sportivas could end their reign.

After speaking to friends and colleagues, it turns out the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX boots are a bit like cilantro — you either love it, or you hate it with a burning passion. But to me, they’re perfect. I like the look of the boots and the available colorways. They look like they mean business when you’re out on the trail.

The boots are perfect for narrow feet, and lace up for a snug, albeit supportive, fit. However, there’s no wide fit option, so those with wide feet need to look elsewhere, such as the Keen Targhee IV.

The upper is made from nubuck leather and a breathable Gore-Tex lining for a water-resistant finish. They coped well with heavy rain and deep puddles, and are also tear-resistant, so they can withstand even the rockiest terrain. The lacing system is very supportive, and cinched in all the right places to ensure a comfortable walk.

Although the laces get tight, my ankles moved freely. In other boots, I’ve been used to having a limited range of movement around my ankles like the Scarpa Cyrus 2 Mid GTX, but these felt a lot more forgiving.

The La Sportiva boots have a footbed boost of 5mm, which is simply the insole height. This contributes to the cushioning of the boot and felt like it contoured to my feet. The drop value of 8mm (from heel to toe) also helped me get the best posture possible.

Usually, in other boots, I experience some strain on my lower back as a result of a smaller drop value, as there’s more pressure on my calves. Instead, I felt supported. The flex system with the CM EVE foam (a lightweight, rubber foam) also helps with rebound.

The outsole provided me with a lot of grip for every terrain I walked on. The lugs of the boot, which dig into the ground to provide traction, measure 4.5mm tall. This is a good height for grip and I find it to be the sweet spot, with most of my Keen boots also sitting in this range. The soles are made of Vibram rubber, so they absorb a lot of the impact of the ground, which helped reduce strain when walking over longer distances.

I have no complaints about the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots and their comfort level. I wore them right out of the box with no issues. My first walk in these boots took me through gravel, muddy fields, and shallow running water. The traction and flex felt great right off the bat.

The toe box of the boots is quite narrow, but this really wasn’t an issue for me. In fact, since my feet are very narrow, the ideal fit gave me more control, providing a more stable hiking experience.

My only very slight qualm is that my feet naturally swell from heat when walking, so the boots can start to feel a little tight. It’s obviously good that the lace-up system doesn’t slip, but sometimes, a little bit of give is a good thing, as you can move more freely. With that said, it didn’t cause me any major pain or blisters.

Cushioning in these boots is ideal. It took away some of the impact, especially when walking over bigger rocks and generally rough terrain, but I could still feel what was going on underfoot. The Scarpa Cyrus 2 Mid boots also let you feel the ground beneath your feet through the soles, and this is a feature I’ve come to really appreciate.

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are easily some of my favorite boots.. They’re comfortable, cushioned, and support me across any terrain. The cushioning helps support my knees by reducing impact.

The 4.5mm lugs on the outsole of the hiking boots made me feel stable across all terrain I walked on. Even on slippery surfaces like wet rocks, the Vibram soles provided a lot of grip, and I didn’t slip once despite my clumsy disposition.

The arch support is great, and this in turn improved my posture. Since the lace-up system is tight for narrow feet, I felt a lot of support from the side walls — these two things combined stopped my feet from turning inward as I walked and boosted protection for my ankles by increasing my overall stability.

The boots have a moderate amount of flex, but never bent too much. I had complete support where I needed it. The most flex is happening in the toe box, which worked perfectly for me, especially when navigating uneven, tricky terrain.

Waterproofing on the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX boots is very effective. I went out hiking in the pouring rain, and my socks stayed completely dry. My walk also took me through puddles and shallow running water, and luckily my feet stayed dry and warm. I know I’ll be able to rely on these boots for all seasons.

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are easy to maintain, just like any other leather boot. If they get muddy on the trail, remove the laces and gently brush off any dry mud. Then, use a damp cloth to remove any stubborn stains. Let the boots air-dry naturally and avoid artificial heat, as it can compromise the boot's integrity.

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are some of my favorite boots. They were comfortable and ready for a long walk right out of the box, and felt durable, even on trickier terrain. The boots provided excellent traction and stability across mud, gravel, and sand, and the waterproofing withstood stormy weather.

Although the cushioning and support are good, it’s worth noting that the boots fit narrowly. For people with wider feet, this boot simply won’t fit even if you size up, and unfortunately, La Sportiva doesn’t offer a wide fit option.

Nevertheless, this is still a great all-rounder boot to support you on the toughest adventures, and one I certainly recommend.

#3315. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

#3314. Why AI Can’t Replace Engineering Teams

How to convince your boss LLMs can’t do it all

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this:

“ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?”

Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?”

I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising.

Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have.

Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this.

That website works great in the demo—under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process.

Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it.

Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage.

Learn how AI models work. If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions.

Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team.

Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter.

I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time.

Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us.

Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that.

The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework.

Looking for a career in quantum computing hardware? An IBM spin-off called Anderon could receive up to $1 billion in funding from the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act for its quantum foundry, established earlier this year. Could Anderon do for quantum hardware what TSMC did for conventional chips?

#3313. Apple offers a military discount, here’s how to get it

If you’re a member of the U.S. military, Apple offers an easy way to save 10% on eligible products and accessories. It’s available to current and veteran members of the U.S. military and their immediate family members living in the same household. While you’ll need to verify your eligibility to access the discount, the process is simple. There are also a few limitations you’ll want to know about before placing an order. Here’s everything you need to know.

A 10% discount is available to current and Veteran members of the US Military, National Guard and Reserve. Immediate family members who reside in the same household are also eligible.

Verification is handled through ID.me. Creating an ID.me account is free, and current military members can verify their service using their .mil email address. Veterans can enter details of their service information for ID.me to verify, or upload images of official documents (such as a DD-214) for ID.me to review and confirm their eligibility. Once you’re verified, your ID.me account can also be used to access military discounts from other retailers and services that support ID.me verification.

Once verified, you can start shopping by visiting Apple’s Store for Veterans and Military. The discount only applies to Apple products and accessories (including Beats) so third-party products aren’t eligible. Apple services, such as Apple Music and iCloud+, are also excluded. Orders can be shipped directly to you, or you can choose in-store pickup if the product is available at a nearby Apple Store.

This is probably the biggest catch. Apple specifically says ACMI isn’t available when shopping through the Veterans and Military Store. You can still earn 3% back in Daily Cash with Apple Card, but you lose the option to finance your purchase at 0% interest over several months. Apple Upgrade also isn’t available when purchasing through the military store.

The only way to get the military discount is to make your purchase through Apple’s website in a browser. The Apple Store app isn’t an option, which means you also can’t take advantage of Apple’s “Get Ready” feature to select your iPhone model, color, storage capacity, and carrier ahead of pre-orders opening. Instead, you’ll have to navigate Apple’s website on launch day, when demand is high and server traffic can make checkout more challenging. Whether the 10% savings is worth giving up the convenience of a potentially quicker checkout is ultimately up to you.

The military discount can’t be combined with carrier promotions or discounts on iPhone purchases. You can still trade in your existing iPhone through Apple and receive the applicable trade-in value, but you can’t take advantage of carrier-specific trade-in offers, like promotions that give you a larger credit when you trade in an eligible device and activate or upgrade a line.

These purchase limits reset on January 1 each year.

Apple’s military discount is a useful perk, especially if you’re buying a product at launch and want to save 10% right away. However, it’s worth comparing prices with other retailers before you buy, since sales and promotions can sometimes beat Apple’s discount. The military store also comes with a few limitations, so you’ll want to weigh the savings against the features and payment options you’re giving up. Even with those caveats, 10% off can make a real difference on an expensive Apple purchase.

#3312. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

#3311. From Chip Lab to Center Stage

This integrated circuit designer explains wearables to consumers

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

IEEE Member Preethi Ashwath is one of the few women who work in analog integrated circuit design, where about 11 percent are female.

Many engineers are more comfortable working behind the scenes developing technology than speaking to consumers about products. But Preethi Ashwath has learned to take center stage, talking about the “hearable” and wearable devices she has had a hand in developing as an analog integrated circuit designer in the consumer electronics division at Analog Devices of Wilmington, Mass.

The IEEE member is one of the few women who work in the specialized field, where about 11 percent are female, according to career platform Zippia.

Preethi Ashwath Employer Analog Devices, in BostonTitle Integrated circuit designerMember grade MemberAlma maters SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

Ashwath stepped out from behind the scenes last year to meet with attendees at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. She demonstrated Analog’s new earbuds, which track people’s heart and lung health through vibrations in their ear canals.

After she demonstrated her ability to explain the technology to consumers in simple terms, Analog selected her to represent the company at other events. She says she has “come to see speaking as part of contributing to the field, rather than something separate from technical work.”

She also gives technical talks on various aspects of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and other topics, as well as participates in panel discussions, she says, because they “reach engineers well beyond my immediate team.”

Ashwath is an active volunteer with the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.

“Whether through designing semiconductor products, publishing technical articles, reviewing conference papers, or speaking at industry events, I try to contribute to the growth of the engineering community and the advancement of the field,” she says.

Ashwath, who grew up in Bengaluru, India, learned about electronics engineering from her high school physics tutor.

That introduction led her to take electronics as one of her core courses in her final years there. At the time, Ashwath’s older sister was pursuing an engineering degree.

“Between my interest in electronics and seeing her already on that path, it became clear to me that engineering was the way to go,” Ashwath says.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in electronics and communications engineering at the SJB Institute of Technology, in Bengaluru, she wanted to pursue a career in very-large-scale integration. But that changed once she moved to the United States and began her master’s program in electrical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.

She discovered her passion for circuits and devices during an internship at Intel in Santa Clara, Calif. She learned about circuit design, package design, and reliability verification tools such as Ansys Totem.

“Seeing every layer of the chip development process gave me a more complete picture of what goes into building a semiconductor product,” she says. “Through that experience, I realized I felt most connected to design.

“It was the hard work and creativity that drew me in. You start with a specification, build a circuit, simulate it, then wait for the chip to come back from fabrication. When your design works, it’s a real feeling of satisfaction. It teaches you patience and perseverance.”

After attaining her master’s degree, she was hired by Intel as an analog design engineer. She gained experience in mixed-signal circuit design before joining Analog. In her current role, she works on consumer hearables such as earbuds and wearables including fitness trackers and health monitors.

Her main focus is designing ESD pad rings, the borders of specialized circuits built around a microchip’s outermost edge to protect it from the discharge, which can damage circuit paths or introduce latent defects that lead to failures later in the chip’s life cycle.

“On a chip with multiple voltage domains, you have to plan how the protection structures are placed and connected across the whole pad ring—and get it right,” Ashwath says. “A mistake there could cause a chip to fail in the field in ways that are very hard to debug afterward.

“It’s detailed work that requires understanding both the device physics and how the whole chip fits together.”

Part of the job is designing and creating an integrated circuit’s building blocks, including ESD protection structures and other mixed-signal blocks. Ashwath conducts rigorous checks to verify they work as intended before being integrated into a chip.

She collaborates with ESD advisors, layout designers, and the digital team that designs the chip’s digital logic.

“I work with them to make sure my analog circuits and their digital blocks work together correctly,” she says. “No two days look exactly the same.”

In 2024 she was recognized with the company’s Impact Award for her “exceptional work on a critical project with significant cross-functional business impact.”

Ashwath was selected to represent Analog at events after a senior leader encouraged her to ask for high-visibility opportunities, she says.

“Most of my time is spent on designing circuits and simulations,” she says. “At CES, I stood in front of customers, engineers, and members of the press, explaining our technology and answering questions on the spot.”

The earbuds she demonstrated monitor minute vibrations from a user’s heart and lungs, according to the Analog website. The vibrations can detect arrhythmia, a leaky heart valve, or fluid in the lungs.

“Hearables are evolving from playing back audio to becoming health-monitoring platforms,” she says. “The ear turns out to be a good location for picking up physiological signals, so these devices can capture vital signs while someone is simply wearing them normally.

“The hard part is achieving high signal quality. The signals you’re trying to detect are very small and buried in the noise from the person’s movements and the surrounding environment.

“That’s where analog front-end design becomes critical. Extracting a meaningful signal from a noisy real-world environment is fundamentally an analog problem.”

Being face-to-face with customers at the conference was new to her.

“What struck me most was seeing how people react to the technology,” she says. “When you’re designing a block, you’re focused on specifications and margins. At CES, after explaining what the product does, I had a better understanding of why it matters to them.

“That connection between the circuit work and the final product is something you don’t always see from the design bench.”

Since the CES, Ashwath has presented other technologies she’s worked on. At the annual National Association of Music Merchants show in Anaheim, Calif., she demonstrated the A2B Automotive Audio Bus to the audio industry. The bus uses a low-cost unshielded twisted-pair cable to carry multichannel digital audio, control data, synchronized clock signals, and power in fewer than 50 microseconds, according to Analog.

“IEEE connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

At the company’s Global Technology Conference—an internal event held in Boston that draws engineers from the company’s more than 50 sites around the world—Ashwath led a demonstration of its solutions for augmented reality smart glasses.

“Each of these events has a different audience,” she says. “Learning to explain my technical work to different people has become a skill I’ve acquired.”

The most rewarding part of her job, she says, is seeing the end result of her work.

“You spend months on a design, and there’s a long wait between finishing it and finding out whether your instincts were right,” she says. “When the measurements match what you simulated, that’s the most satisfying moment in this job.

“The other part is knowing my work ends up in a real product. The circuits I design go into devices people actually use every day.”

Like many engineers, Ashwath joined IEEE to access research published in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. It keeps her current in a field that keeps moving, she says.

During her first year of membership, in 2021, she discovered other perks including networking and educational opportunities.

“IEEE connects you to a community outside your own company,” she says. “Attending lectures and technical talks exposes you to approaches and problems you wouldn’t encounter in your own work.”

She eventually began seeking out volunteer opportunities, specifically with IEEE conferences and journals, because they are “how you stay current with what’s happening in circuits and systems beyond your own day-to-day work,” she says.

“As an analog designer,” she says, “being connected to that broader community matters. The field moves, and you need a way to keep learning from it.”

She serves as a peer reviewer of papers for several IEEE conferences including the IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and the IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems. ISCAS is the flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. MWSCAS is the oldest U.S. conference on the technologies.

“Someone has to assess whether submitted work is technically sound and worth presenting,” she says, “and that only happens if practicing engineers are willing to put in the time.”

The combination of learning from the community and contributing to it is what makes her membership worthwhile, she says.

“Analog design is a field where you’re always learning. Just when you feel you understand one architecture, there’s another one to learn,” she says. “Being an active learner isn’t optional in this field; it’s the requirement, and being part of the IEEE community helps with that.

“IEEE also connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry.

“Reviewing papers means reading what researchers are working on, which is often quite different from how the same problems get approached in a product environment. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3309. 10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: big sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and big ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the new crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things quickly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

Stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3306. The Apple Watch's New 'Siri Recap' Feature Is Even Creepier Than I Expected

The “Siri Recap” feature that Apple announced in September is finally available in a developer beta, and I’ve spent the last 24 hours with the feature turned on. It’s even more unsettling than the “Live Rewind” feature that launched at the same time. It listens to all my conversations, and produces summaries that are both helpful and deeply creepy.

I have a button in the watch’s Control Center that can turn the recapping abilities off, but if I forget to do so, Siri listens to everything. I’ll get a recap of my entire evening, presented in roughly hour-long chunks, including things I would have completely forgotten I had even heard about.

The recaps somberly mention silly memes my kids were laughing about, and make major bullet points out of offhand remarks from brief conversations. If a conversation sticks to a single topic, I’ll often get a reasonably good summary of it, with specific facts and numbers highlighted; but just as often, Siri will get confused and mix up several topics or completely mishear a name or phrase.

Apple has four features that it considers part of “audio intelligence":

Music recognition, better known as Shazam. We’ve had a version of this on the Apple Watch for a long time now, although it has some improvements and now identifies music automatically.

Sound recognition, which can notify you about doorbells and babies crying. A version of this launched in 2020 as an accessibility feature.

Live Rewind, which gives you an on-wrist transcript of the last 15 seconds of detected speech.

Siri Recaps, which summarizes entire conversations for you to read on your phone.

Live Rewind had the flashiest demo from the Apple event: A server rattled off the day’s specials at a restaurant, and then the Apple Watch-wearing diner checked his watch to see a readout of exactly which dishes had just been mentioned. The utility is both obvious and kind of unnecessary: Why wouldn’t you just ask the server to repeat the list while they’re standing right there?

I haven’t found myself using Live Rewind, except out of curiosity about how the feature works. I discovered that it doesn’t pick up song lyrics very well, and also that by the time I think to check what was just said in a conversation, more than 15 seconds has passed since the part I was unsure about. I haven’t yet found a reason to use it for real.

But Siri Recaps? Those are both useful and unsettling. I enabled the feature, and decided to test it out later. But since it was on, it dutifully listened in as I picked up my son from school and gave him an update on an ailing family member’s health. We stopped by the library, and along the way we chatted about a variety of things: holiday travel plans, library policies, and the possibility of humans living in space in the future. Siri was listening to it all.

At least for now, the feature is only available in a developer beta, so sign up for that now if you want to try it. You'll need an Apple Watch Series 12 (or Ultra 4) and an iPhone 16 or better, excluding the 16e. (I have a 16 Pro, so I'm good.)

After you're updated to 27.3, go into the Watch app, tap Siri, and turn on Siri Recap. You can set a schedule for when it should listen (for example, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., if you want it on for the work day but off for the evening). You'll need to set a passcode on your watch, and you'll be guided through a step to upgrade your audio connection. The control center on the watch will have a button you can use to turn Siri recaps on and off at will. To read your recaps, go to the Siri app on your phone.

But still: I feel weird publishing the contents of these recaps, because they do contain things that people said to me in what they assumed was a private setting. I had the feature on when I attended a choir practice, and Siri recapped the brief chats I had with other choir members before and after practice. (Interestingly, it did not recap any of the quiet conversations I had with fellow sopranos while the tenors were rehearsing their part. I’m not sure if the watch was unable to hear us over the music, or if Siri is programmed not to listen when music is being played.)

Because speakers aren’t identified, it seems Siri doesn’t know what to do when there is a disagreement. A human note-taker would jot down that Person A made a point in favor of something, and person B made a point against. But when my son and I disagreed about how likely space colonization might be in the future, the recap didn’t reflect the separate positions that were put forth. It summarized the conversation as including “debating the feasibility and timeline of human space colonization and asteroid mining,” which isn’t exactly accurate, but close enough.

When it comes to the content of the discussion, the recap notes a bullet point of “skepticism regarding permanent space colonies within the next 100 years.” It didn’t include my reasons for being skeptical, and didn’t mention my son’s opposing viewpoint at all. If I were using this recap to jog my memory of the conversation, it wouldn’t be all that helpful.

Details are sometimes egregiously incorrect. After a discussion about a family member’s health, the recap had notes on the prognosis of “father.” The family member we discussed is not anybody’s father. Names in general seem to be a problem; I recommended a book to my son, and the recap includes notes about the content of the book, but not its title. The book’s author appears in the introduction to the recap (sort of a summary of a summary), but not in the content of the recap itself where the book is mentioned.

I should probably turn Siri recaps off. It seems wrong to let people chat with me without letting them know that their conversation is being ... well, not technically recorded, but basically recorded.

But it’s so tempting to leave it on so that I can review my day. Some of the details in the recaps are useful, like the dates that were discussed as options for a holiday party. The recaps will be deleted in about a week (unless I save them to the notes app), so if I want to remind myself of a conversation a few days ago, I should be able to scroll back through my recaps and find it.

I would be a fool to rely on the recaps, though. The most important points of a conversation are often left out; Siri doesn’t know what’s actually important, and there’s no way to guide it as to what to pay attention to. Specific details can be wrong, as I mentioned. There’s also no way to control when a “conversation” starts or stops, unless you are turning the recap feature on and off from the watch.

And there’s more: Not only are names usually omitted (wait, who did she say I should ask about that project?), the few identifiers that make it into the recap, like names of events, are often wrong. Subjects of discussion are often conflated in really unhelpful ways: My husband mentioned paying for certain course registrations for one of our children, and later I talked to that child about an unrelated exam. The recap got all of these things mixed up with each other and was wrong about pretty much every detail. About all the recap could usefully do is to remind me that something about AP U.S. History was discussed. Reading the recaps can be like reliving your day entirely in the passive voice.

#3305. Apple reportedly met with Thai officials over spyware alerts sent to politicians

Bloomberg reports that Apple has met with Thai government officials in the wake of its recent wave of iPhone alerts about mercenary spyware attacks. Here are the details.

Last week, The Financial Times and TechCrunch reported that Apple had sent a fresh wave of threat notifications to potential spyware targets in 99 countries, warning them that they may have been targeted by mercenary spyware attacks.

At the time, the FT focused on German lawmakers who had received the warnings, while TechCrunch highlighted recipients in other countries, including Beirut-based filmmaker Radwan Mortada.

Today, Bloomberg reported that “Thailand held meetings with Apple Inc. officials” over the notifications, adding that the warnings raised questions about “who may have targeted [Thai politicians] and why.”

Receiving an alert doesn’t necessarily mean a device was successfully compromised, Digital Economy and Society Minister Chaichanok Chidchob said after meeting Apple representatives Wednesday, Krungthep Turakij and other media reported. Thai authorities also have no evidence so far that the latest attempted attacks involved Pegasus, the spyware developed by Israel’s NSO Group, he said.

As Bloomberg explains, Pegasus was “allegedly used against pro-democracy campaigners in 2022.”

The recent wave of alerts, which were sent out on October 29, followed another round in August, when Apple notified potential targets in 110 countries. As always, Apple declined to disclose what triggers these notifications to prevent attackers from evading detection in the future, but recommended that recipients enable Lockdown Mode and seek expert security assistance.

Bloomberg added that Thai authorities are expected to meet with other technology companies on Thursday to discuss potential countermeasures, including risks to Android devices.

#3304. 10 Hacks Every Reddit User Should Know

If you're looking for discussions, recommendations, or advice online, it's hard to avoid Reddit. From mainstream sports to niche crafts, it does seem that there's some kind of Reddit community for everyone. (And if there's not one, you can make one yourself.) If you're using Reddit, here are 10 hacks you should know about to improve your experience on the site.

Reddit used to let everyone view your post and comment history, but in recent years, you can make your profile private. You can hide your posts, comments, and the subreddits you're a part of. If you want to do this, click your profile icon once you've logged in to Reddit, and go to Settings > Profile. Alternatively, you can follow the direct link to Reddit's profile settings page. Click the drop-down menu next to Content & Activity, and select Hide all. You should also turn off Online Status on the same page to stop people from seeing when you're using Reddit.

Old Reddit lets you use the site's classic design, and I prefer it to the more modern UI. Old Reddit looks dated, but it doesn't have infinite scrolling, distracting animations, and a bunch of features designed to increase the time you spend on the platform. It's no wonder that Reddit is making it harder to access this version of the site. As long as it's around, you should switch to Old Reddit for a cleaner reading experience. You can do that by going to Reddit Settings > Preferences and enabling Default to Old Reddit. You can also visit old.reddit.com, though you'll need to sign in for access

Many subreddits use custom themes that range from beautiful to borderline unusable. If you want a more consistent UI across the site, you should disable these custom subreddit styles. Go to Reddit Settings > Preferences and turn off Use community themes. If you're using Old Reddit, click the preferences button in the top-right corner, and under "display options," disable allow subreddits to show me custom themes.

A multireddit is a feed that shows posts from a customized group of subreddits. You can think of it as a way to break out of Reddit's algorithms, and create your own Reddit feed. I use multireddits to follow all sports-related subs I'm interested in. I even have one for gaming, and one for fountain pens. It's a great way to create interest-specific feeds, and if you make them private, no one else can see them. To create one, click the Create custom feed button in the left pane in new Reddit. In the Old Reddit design, click the Create button in the left pane. Be sure to select the Private button to keep it from showing up for others. You can add as many subreddits as you like to the list, and bookmark the feed to access it whenever you wish to.

Reddit has recently adopted an Instagram-like experience for its feeds. It removed the ability to sort posts by new, controversial, best, etc., and instead offers "For You" and "Following." If you dislike this change, you can bypass it. I use Reddit on mobile Safari, and I recommend an extension called Sink It for Reddit. It can automatically redirect you to Old Reddit, and there's a feature that optimizes it for mobile, which brings back the old sorting options. You can also use third-party apps such as RedReader for Android, or RDX for Reddit on an iPhone or iPad to restore the old sorting options for Reddit posts.

After all these years, Reddit's built-in search still leaves something to be desired—at least, on the surface. To find posts on Reddit faster, use search filters on the site. For instance, adding "title:" to your search will limit the results to post titles, and boolean operators such as AND, OR, and NOT also work for advanced searches on the site.
