#3177. How Microcredentials Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program offers ethics and compliance training

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

#3176. Top Wall Street analysts are confident about the growth prospects of these 3 stocks

Geopolitical uncertainty and macroeconomic pressures have continued to affect market sentiment in recent trading sessions. But continued volatility also presents an opportunity to find stocks trading at attractive prices and benefit from their long-term growth potential.

Recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help investors gain key insights and pick the right stocks. These experts assign ratings after performing an in-depth analysis of a company's strengths and weaknesses, while also paying attention to macro factors.

In his latest research note, Bank of America analyst Koji Ikeda reiterated a buy rating on Snowflake, Datadog, JFrog, MongoDB, and Twilio. The analyst has a price target of $300 on SNOW. "MDB is leading the shift to cloud-native, AI-powered data infrastructure management with Atlas-driven scale, expanding cash generation and strong long-term upside potential," said the analyst.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that MDB is consistently winning market share in a huge, durable database market as enterprises modernize applications and shift workloads from legacy systems to cloud-based ecosystems. He believes that with the growth in Atlas, MDB's multi-cloud Database-as-a-Service (DBaaS) offering, the shift in mix toward higher-margin, recurring subscription revenue and disciplined expense management is driving higher cash flows and expanding free cash flow margins.

Feinseth contends that MongoDB deserves a premium valuation in terms of revenue and cash flow multiples compared to its infrastructure software peers, given its above-market, top-line growth, enhanced unit economics and growing cash generation.

Feinseth further highlighted that MongoDB benefits from a strong competitive moat, driven by its flexible document-based architecture, extensive developer adoption and broad, multi-cloud Atlas footprint. The 5-star analyst emerged from the meeting more bullish on Walmart, citing the strength of the company's growth strategy and long-term prospects. Specifically, Thomas believes that Walmart is the leader, and continues to invest, in delivery speed. The analyst is optimistic about further improvement in Walmart's delivery times and costs, driven by continued investment, growth in e-commerce and store-fulfilled delivery orders, and improving order density.

Further, Thomas expects automation to lower fulfillment costs. In fact, Walmart highlighted that automation of the U.S. business is now about 60% complete. The analyst expects the rollout to be completed in the next several years.

#3175. iOS 27.3 adds three new features I’ve used almost every day

iOS 27.3 is coming next month, and during the beta so far there are three new features I’ve been using almost every day.

Siri AI in iOS 27 brings major upgrades by providing world knowledge, personal context features, and being more conversational than ever. But one previously announced Siri improvement—an expanded set of actions for Apple apps—didn’t make the cut in iOS 27.0.

Now in iOS 27.3, though, Apple is rolling out its first set of new app actions for Siri AI.

Siri AI has new capabilities across apps like Calendar, Files, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It’s a big step toward making voice-driven computing more powerful on Apple platforms, and I’ve had fun experimenting with everything new Siri can do.

Read more: iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps

Apple Health gets a big overhaul in iOS 27.3, with a fresh design and new features that utilize Apple Intelligence for more personalized health insights. Per Apple:

The updated experience includes a new Insights tab that surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.

In my testing so far, I’ve especially enjoyed getting up-to-date guidance every day on my health metrics, browsing the deep collection of new educational videos and articles, and understanding all the factors that contribute to longevity. I think Apple is moving the right direction with this update.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here

If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4, iOS 27.3 adds a powerful new feature called Siri Recap that “ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory.”

Siri Recap functions like an outsourced short-term memory reserve. The data it collects is saved inside the Siri app in a new Recaps tab, where it lives for seven days and is then deleted—unless you manually save a specific recap.

So far in the beta, I’ve found the summaries Siri generates to strike a good balance of being helpful but not too invasive. It reminds me of key details, but there’s nothing I’ve seen that feels overly sensitive or personalized. That may change over time the more I use it, but so far I think this could prove a really valuable feature.

Read more: watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love

#3173. Perplexity brings AI agents feature called Teammates to the Mac

This week, Perplexity has deployed its new proactive agentic AI feature called Teammates to the Mac. Perplexity Teammates were previously limited to iOS and the web.

Similar to Grok Bot, Perplexity Teammates are task-oriented proactive agentic AI threads that work for you without constantly being prompted. Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots are similar, but use a single chat model rather than supporting multiple instances.

Teammates are a team of AI agents that own ongoing work. Give a teammate a responsibility, such as managing a growth campaign, triaging incoming bug reports, tracking your metrics, or researching a new market, and it owns that work around the clock. It plans the tasks, brings in more agents when the work grows, and follows through until the result is ready for your review.

Access to Teammates currently requires a paid Perplexity Max subscription. The feature builds on top of Perplexity’s existing AI orchestration system.

Mike DePasquale: Thank you, David, and good morning, everyone. I'll start with an overview of the quarter and our business. Ceci will then take you through the financials, and we'll close by taking your questions. Our third quarter results reflect the strength of our core software business. License fee revenue grew 39% year-over-year, and that high-margin recurring revenue lifted our gross margin to 90% from 77% a year ago, and helped reduce our operating loss by 8%. Our gross margin has improved every quarter since the second quarter of last year, and license fee revenue has now grown by double digits on a year-over-year basis for the past three consecutive quarters.

Total revenue for the quarter was down 4% from last year's third quarter, as strong license growth largely offset lower hardware sales. The third quarter is typically our slowest period of the year due to summer vacation schedules, and the first quarter tends to benefit from license renewal activity. For the first nine months of 2026, total revenue rose 14%, and our net loss has improved by 42%, a solid step in the right direction. I want to spend a moment on why we're seeing growing new business wins and how they relate to our core biometric expertise built over decades, which is gaining recognition as a real differentiator where identity assurance matters most.

Areas such as government, defense, and financial services, the regulated industries, these customers know how, with uncertainty, that a person, the actual individual accessing a critical system, is who they claim to be. That's what our Identity-Bound Biometrics deliver, tying access to the individual rather than to a device, a phone, a token, or a password that can be shared, stolen, or phished. Regulators are increasingly pushing in this direction. In response to growing incidents of systems compromise, in the UAE, for example, the central bank directed banks and other licensed financial institutions to phase out SMS and email one-time passwords earlier this year in favor of stronger methods, including biometrics and passkeys.

Policies like these are important tailwinds for the value our solutions provide. That backdrop is showing up in who's choosing BIO-key and in the size of the opportunities. Our international team is increasingly winning larger, high-profile deals in highly regulated sectors, as I mentioned before, such as government and banking. In the third quarter, the Central Bank of Jordan selected BIO-key for a national biometric authentication initiative to modernize how clients access digital services across the financial sector, which serves roughly 11.6 million people. We're working closely with the central bank as the initiative moves towards development deployment.

In Portugal, a national security agency selected BIO-key and our partner, Visualforma, to secure access to its administrative systems, privileged accounts, and critical applications. We are seeing incredible upside in the international markets, in particular in the Middle East and in Europe. These awards bring us to eight new Middle East region customers in roughly seven months. These are among the most security-conscious organizations anywhere, and each deployment becomes an important proof of concept and reference for the next, and that's what we're seeing now. This traction is built on strong local distribution and integration partners with strong connections and understanding of each customer's needs.

We continue to expand our partner network, such as our recent partnership with Al Majlis Group to extend our reach across the Arabian Gulf. We have also begun establishing a BIO-key subsidiary in Saudi Arabia to support our growing government business there that will also be staffed with BIO-key resources. Overall, the opportunity is very large, and Gartner forecasts end-user information security spending in the Middle East and North Africa will reach approximately $4 billion in 2026. It's starting to be reflected in our results as the third quarter revenue from our Europe, Middle East, and South America region grew 39% with license fees more than doubling.

In Europe, we recently launched a technology integration with Cipher, the cybersecurity division of global security group Prosegur, bringing our IAM, biometric, and password technologies into their portfolio, starting in Portugal with plans to explore other markets where they operate, such as in Spain, the U.S., and in Brazil. In the U.S., our focus is on PortalGuard, our flexible IAM platform supporting 16 factors of authentication, including fingerprint, face, and palm biometrics. We continue to roll out our latest version, PortalGuard 7, across our customer base. In October, we recruited cybersecurity veteran Steve Morrow as President of PortalGuard to accelerate adoption.

We are sharpening our U.S. go-to-market efforts through our DLT partnership, which is focused on the public sector, as well as with other channel partners on the commercial side. Benefits for these efforts are already taking shape. Earlier this week, we announced that a major U.S. casino resort selected PortalGuard and our Identity-Bound Biometrics to secure workforce access across its 24/7 operations, marking our entry into the gaming and hospitality industry. This enterprise-wide prepaid three-year agreement was won against much larger competitors who were unable to provide the functionality we have. Most of the resort's highest value employees can't carry phones on the gaming floor, making our efficient biometric-driven solution a natural fit.

In the realm of AI, our new internally developed Passkey:YOU authenticator received full FIDO Alliance certification this September. It is now in final testing ahead of its major launch, which will allow us to leapfrog the capabilities of our earlier outsourced solution. Our Passkey:YOU solution lets employees sign in with a fingerprint scanner or badge rather than a phone or a token, and it positions us for one of the most important emerging identity challenge, AI agents. Machine identities, including AI agents, now outnumber human identities by over 100:1. It's an amazing statistics, and that's according to industry research. This year, the FIDO Alliance formed a working group to develop standards for trusted AI agent interactions.

We believe that for the highest risk actions, the answer has to be verified human, not password or device acknowledgment. Our Identity-Bound Biometrics can tie approval of sensitive AI-driven actions to the actual person accountable. This agentic AI authentication and authorization is an important aspect of the integrated offering of our new Cipher relationship. Steve Morrow, as I mentioned, the President of our PortalGuard group, is leading the development of the product plans in this area. We see this as a meaningful new market opportunity alongside our core workforce and customer authentication business. On the financial side, we strengthened our balance sheet considerably in the third quarter.

We retired our remaining note and debt, leaving us effectively debt-free, and we currently have a solid cash and working capital position to fund our business. Looking ahead, our recent wins, growing base of recurring license revenue, and a solid pipeline of regulated industry opportunities across EMEA position us for a solid finish to 2026 and a really strong start to 2027, supported by the annual license renewal of our largest customer, which exceeds $1 million. We expect roughly $1.2 million in annual license fee renewals in the first quarter alone, and we are targeting profitability as we approach that timeframe.

Our deep biometric expertise, marquee government and financial customers, growing high-margin software revenue, streamlined cost structure, and cleaner balance sheet gives us a very strong foundation, and we believe it sets the stage for an exciting future period. I will hand the call over to Ceci to take you through the financials in more detail. Ceci?

I suspect with the new legislative changes past election here last week, we are going to see a lot more pressure to reel that in and ensure that we are securing and locking down agents so they do not go rogue.

First up is a sci-fi thriller from “It Follows” director David Robert Mitchell, in which an entire 1980s suburban neighborhood, Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor are yanked out of reality and dropped into a world full of dinosaurs. Yeah, we're not sure how that works either, but it sounds like a good time to us.

From there, things get a lot sillier with 2024’s notorious Spider-Man spin-off that bombed so spectacularly it’s since become a hilariously watchable, so-bad-it’s-good cult favorite, with Dakota Johnson as a paramedic who can suddenly see the future. There are plenty of unbelievable happenings in this movie, and you'll love the blissfully baffling decisions made throughout.

And then, something totally different: A 2013 documentary and one of the most beloved behind-the-scenes stories ever told, chronicling director Alejandro Jodorowsky’s wildly ambitious, ultimately doomed 1970s attempt to adapt Frank Herbert’s “Dune.” No Timothée Chalamet here.

There you have it. Clear your schedule and grab the popcorn, because these three newly added HBO Max movies are everything you need to get the party started this weekend.

What is it about? From David Robert Mitchell, the writer-director behind the cult horror hit “It Follows" comes a story about...dinosaurs? Set in a small 1982 suburb, “The End of Oak Street” follows the Platt family, headed by Denise (Anne Hathaway) and Greg (Ewan McGregor), whose ordinary neighborhood is suddenly thrown into turmoil by a mysterious cosmic event and dropped into a prehistoric world teeming with dinosaurs. Stranded in a world they don’t recognize, the family and their neighbors have to band together to survive the terrifying new dangers lurking around every corner.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Why you should watch it: Produced by J.J. Abrams, this is a Spielbergian blend of wonder and horror expertly mixed together. It's a great little thrill ride that mixes familiar “Jurassic Park”-style scares with a side of confused family, which makes for a surprisingly fun movie.

Watch "The End of Oak Street" on HBO Max now

What is it about? “Madame Web” takes a weird detour into the stranger corners of the Spider-Man universe. Dakota Johnson stars as Cassandra Webb, a New York City paramedic who, after a near-death experience, suddenly develops the power to see the future. When her visions reveal that three young women, played by Sydney Sweeney, Isabela Merced, and Celeste O’Connor, are being hunted by a mysterious, spider-powered killer (Tahar Rahim), Cassie becomes their only protector. To save them, she’ll have to understand her strange new abilities, along with the secrets of her late mother’s past.

Why you should watch it: Let’s be honest: “Madame Web” was a legendary box-office flop that critics tore apart on release. It's since become a hilarious watch even for fans of the character. But that’s exactly why you should watch it. And despite a mostly bad script and even worse acting, there are plenty of moments that will stick with you once it ends. And you'll want to make sure you're in the know for any potential future Sony/Marvel universe lore, too.

What is it about? Before Denis Villeneuve or David Lynch took a crack at Frank Herbert’s “Dune,” Chilean-French filmmaker Alejandro Jodorowsky nearly made the most audacious version of all. This documentary tells the true story of that doomed 1970s production, which Jodorowsky envisioned as a mind-expanding sci-fi epic. Through interviews with the director himself, the documentary charts how he assembled a jaw-dropping team, including artists H.R. Giger and Moebius, effects wizard Dan O’Bannon, a score by Pink Floyd, and a planned cast featuring Salvador Dalí, Orson Welles, and Mick Jagger, only to watch it collapse when no studio would finance it.

Why you should watch it: Even though his film was never made, Jodorowsky’s ideas and artwork went on to shape sci-fi landmarks like “Alien,” “Blade Runner”, and “Star Wars", making this a must-watch for fans. With “Dune: Part Three” on the horizon, there’s no better time to revisit the greatest “Dune” movie that never was.

#3169. Epic formally asks SCOTUS to uphold contempt ruling against Apple

Epic Games has submitted its official response to Apple’s Supreme Court appeal, urging the justices to uphold the contempt ruling over App Store payment restrictions. Here are the details.

As most 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple and Epic Games have been engaged in a lengthy legal battle since 2020, when Epic sued Apple after Fortnite was removed from the App Store.

The move came after Epic remotely activated an alternative payment system that bypassed Apple’s In-App Purchase system.

Although the court largely sided with Apple, it did rule that the company could no longer prevent developers from directing users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple ultimately allowed those links, but imposed new restrictions, including a 27% commission on external purchases, in addition to new rules limiting how developers could display buttons and links to alternative payment methods.

Epic challenged those restrictions, and the court agreed that Apple had violated the original injunction, holding the company in civil contempt.

Apple has since attempted multiple times to overturn that ruling, arguing that the original injunction contained no explicit prohibition on imposing those restrictions.

Epic, on the other hand, argues that Apple deliberately circumvented the court order by introducing new rules designed to achieve the same result as those originally prohibited.

In May, Apple appealed to the Supreme Court, which agreed in June to hear the case. Apple submitted its opening brief in September, followed by supporting briefs from the U.S. government and several legal and business groups.

Those included the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Chamber of Progress, and several former federal antitrust enforcers. In a nutshell, the U.S. government argued that the original injunction did not clearly prohibit Apple’s 27% commission on external purchases, but maintained that the company was correctly held in contempt for restricting how developers could display external payment buttons.

In its opening brief, Apple argues, citing multiple legal precedents, that courts must enforce the letter of an injunction rather than its broader spirit.

According to the company, there was nothing in the original injunction explicitly prohibiting it from charging commissions on external purchases or imposing additional restrictions on payment links, so it should not be held in contempt for conduct that the court order did not clearly prohibit.

In its response filed today, Epic disputes Apple’s interpretation of the injunction, arguing that the company “attempts to avoid contempt by proposing an extreme legal standard.”

[Apple] argues that a court can find contempt only if an injunction spells out the exact practice at issue–so an injunction barring Apple’s then-existing anti-steering rules left it free to implement new ones that prevent steering just as effectively. Nothing in this Court’s precedents supports that approach, which would reduce injunctions to a never-ending game of whack-a-mole.

Epic argues that “Apple devised a plan to circumvent the injunction,” claiming that “Apple chose a rate of 27% for the commission, knowing that, when combined with the developers’ payment-handling costs (more than 3%), the rate for linked-out purchases would be higher than the rate for purchases using Apple’s payment system.”

As an Apple executive admitted, every “linked-out transaction is going to be more expensive to any developer * * * than an IAP transaction at 30 percent.” Apple simultaneously commissioned a “sham” report to try to provide an economic justification for the commission; the report contained an “entirely manufactured” rationale for the 27% rate.

The company also argues that “Apple tried to cover up its scheme to circumvent the injunction” by asserting privilege over more than 57,000 documents, and points to Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers’ finding that “its Vice President of Finance ‘outright lied under oath’ when he testified about when Apple decided to impose the new commission.”

Finally, Epic asks the Supreme Court to uphold the contempt ruling against Apple or, if the justices decide to clarify the legal standard for contempt, to send the case back to the lower courts for reconsideration under that standard.

With Epic’s response now filed, Apple has until December 14 to submit its final brief before oral arguments take place on January 11, 2027.

#3165. SpaceX Could Announce a Deal for Tesla as Soon as December. Here's What It Would Do to SpaceX Stock.

Tesla would add around two-thirds of the combined sales. What would that do to the rocket maker's growth?

SpaceX (SPCX -0.59%) and Tesla (TSLA -1.82%) have moved on to haggling over price and control in their merger talks, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, Nov. 12. A deal could be announced as soon as December, the report said, but early 2027 is possible too. And it's shaping up as SpaceX taking over Tesla, with Tesla investors getting SpaceX shares. Neither company commented.

The sizes alone make this unusual. At roughly $140 a share as of this writing, SpaceX is worth about $1.9 trillion, and Tesla, near $397, is worth almost $1.6 trillion.

So, what would a deal do to SpaceX stock? At these prices, it could nearly double SpaceX's share count and leave its shareholders owning a company whose sales come mainly from Tesla. I think the second part matters more than the first.

Buying Tesla at its market value, without a premium, takes around 11.2 billion new SpaceX shares. SpaceX had around 13.6 billion Class A and Class B shares outstanding as of Oct. 15, according to its quarterly filing, so the count could grow around 83%.

This leaves today's SpaceX shareholders with about 55% of the combined company. Tesla holders, of course, will probably want a premium. At a 25% premium, SpaceX's current owners wind up with slightly less than half.

"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," CEO Elon Musk said about a merger on SpaceX's Oct. 20 earnings call. He added shareholders have to back it.

On SpaceX's side, the filing says any deal requires approval from its special committee, board, and controlling shareholder.

SpaceX's third-quarter revenue climbed 161% year over year to $14.6 billion, but Tesla's was flat at $28.0 billion. Put those reports together, and Tesla makes up around 66% of the combined total. Tesla's automotive revenue alone is about 48%. And the AI business SpaceX calls superintelligence shrinks from around half of SpaceX's sales to about 18% of the combined figure.

On those numbers, combined revenue rose only about 27% year over year.

Profit points the other way. SpaceX's third-quarter operating income was $2.8 billion, up from a loss the year before, while Tesla's dropped 56% to $718 million. So Tesla brings around two-thirds of the sales but only about a fifth of the operating income. The combined operating margin is about 8%, versus about 19% for SpaceX alone.

Granted, Tesla's slice of the sales has been shrinking fast. In the third quarter of 2025, Tesla's share of the two companies' combined revenue was around 83%. That stepped down to about 78% in the second quarter of 2026 and about 66% last quarter.

Plus, SpaceX management expects first-quarter 2027 revenue of $33 billion to $37 billion. If Tesla's sales hold around $28 billion a quarter, SpaceX alone could be the bigger half by early next year.

Put another way, SpaceX shareholders would arguably be giving about 45% of their faster growth to owners of a company whose sales were flat last quarter.

Ring-fencing Tesla's China business is one of the key hurdles, Bloomberg reported. It's a sensitive pairing with SpaceX, which serves government customers through Starlink and launched NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope last quarter.

And China isn't a small part of Tesla. The carmaker's third-quarter revenue there was $5.2 billion, down 8% year over year and around 19% of its total. In the combined company, China is about 12% of sales.

Until investors learn how that business is handled, it's tough to tell exactly what SpaceX shareholders might be getting for their shares.

On paper, yes. At market prices, the two companies combined are worth around $3.5 trillion, or about 20 times annualized third-quarter sales. SpaceX alone costs around 33 times its annualized sales.

But the lower sales multiple comes from adding a slower, lower-margin business, not from a cheaper valuation on SpaceX's own growth.

In the end, I think a deal at current prices could make SpaceX a much bigger company and a much slower-growing one. A premium for Tesla holders would just make the trade worse for SpaceX owners.

For SpaceX shareholders, I don't think it looks like a bargain. How much of the company they'd hand over still depends on terms neither side has announced.

The Federal Reserve indicated the possibility of a rate hike this year after its latest meeting, which could have implications for income-seeking investors.

Given this backdrop, dividend-paying stocks with strong yields and upside potential could help investors earn attractive returns.

Backed by solid research, top Wall Street analysts can provide key insights to pick stocks having the ability to generate compelling capital appreciation and pay consistent dividends, driven by solid fundamentals.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Kinetik is a midstream company operating in the Delaware basin. With a quarterly dividend of 81 cents per share (annualized dividend of $3.24 per share), KNTK stock offers a dividend yield of about 7%.

RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on Kinetik stock and increased her price target to $53 from $50, citing expected growth from the KL2 project and sour gas opportunity in New Mexico. Scotto updated her estimates to reflect Kinetik's Q1 2026 results, with adjusted EBITDA beating estimates, driven by improved margins and Gulf Coast marketing gains that offset Waha price-related shut-ins.

The five-star analyst expects the Waha price-related shut-ins to persist until incremental takeaway capacity comes online later this year. Scotto said that Kinetik is well-positioned to capture New Mexico sour gas growth prospects when prices support activity. She sees the Northern Delaware Basin in New Mexico as a major growth opportunity for Kinetik. Scotto highlighted that Kinetik has purpose-built its system for sour gas handling, giving it an edge over new competitors that may face permitting delays of at least three years to build acid gas injection wells.

Additionally, Scotto pointed out Kinetik's attractive capital return framework, which targets a 3.5x to 4.0x leverage ratio, 3% to 5% hike in annual dividend until dividend coverage reaches 1.6x, and opportunistic share buybacks.

"We still view KNTK as a logical takeout candidate for buyers seeking to increase equity NGL barrels and sour gas processing," said Scotto.

Oilfield services company SLB (SLB), formerly known as Schlumberger, is this week's second dividend pick. The company announced a quarterly cash dividend of nearly 30 cents per share, payable on July 9. At an annualized dividend of $1.18 per share, SLB stock offers a dividend yield of 2.5%.

Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on SLB stock with a price target of $63, saying that he believes the company is "positioned to capitalize on long-term opportunities in oilfield activity globally triggered by the ongoing disruptions and shifting supply dynamics in the Middle East."

The five-star analyst expects SLB's dominant position in the international oilfield services market to bolster its earnings power over the long term, supported by increased activity levels over the medium to long term.

Given management's commentary on accelerated exploration activity in regions such as Latin America, Africa and Asia, and his expectation for accelerated final investment decisions in deepwater projects in West Africa, the Gulf of America and Brazil, Mehta expects SLB to benefit from higher services activity needed amid increasing drilling and production.

Mohan added that AI tailwinds are most evident in IBM's Z mainframe offering, where program-to-program growth has increased from 110% several generations ago to the range of 120% to 125% in the prior cycle and roughly 135% for Z17. This acceleration is driven by AI workloads moving beyond fraud detection into inferencing areas like insurance, actuarial modeling, and transaction-level intelligence.

#3163. Tired of paying for cloud storage every month? pCloud’s Black Friday Lifetime deal is the cure for subscription fatigue

Software used to be a one-time purchase, but over time, with the addition of cloud storage and services, everything has become a subscription. One company even tried to make your car seat heaters a subscription. Count the subscriptions you’re paying for right now: iCloud, a password manager, a couple of streaming services, a music service, maybe a VPN, and whatever other app decided this year that it needed to be $4.99 per month for something that used to be a one-time purchase.

Everything is a service now, and a lot of people are hitting the point where one more monthly charge is one too many on principle alone. Cloud storage is the one that’s hardest to cancel, because your photos and files are in it. That’s exactly why pCloud’s Lifetime plans are worth a look this Black Friday: you pay once, and your storage is yours for life!

Apple gives you 5 GB of iCloud for free, which stops being enough about a week after you buy an iPhone. The irony is that they launched with 5 GB of free storage in 2011, and it’s almost laughable that it hasn’t been increased since.

After that, it’s a subscription forever. The 2 TB iCloud+ plan costs $9.99 a month, about $120 a year, for as long as you want your photos to stay where they are. pCloud’s math is different. The 2 TB Lifetime plan is a one-time payment that costs less than four years of iCloud+ at the same size, and the day you buy it is the last day you pay anything for it.

If you’ve been paying for iCloud or Google Drive storage for all of your files for the last 9 years instead of using pCloud, go do the math on how much you’ve spent.

Apple charges a lot to move from a 256 GB MacBook Air to a 512 GB one, and you can’t change your mind later with a hard drive upgrade. Storage has gotten incredibly pricey in recent years as well. pCloud Drive is your solution without breaking the bank. It’s a native Mac app that mounts your pCloud storage as a drive in Finder, so your files appear as if they’re natively on your Mac but live in the cloud until you open them. A 256 GB laptop with a 2 TB pCloud Drive behind it stops feeling small. It runs on macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, and Android, and everything stays in sync across all of them in real time.

With pCloud Backup, backing up the folders you choose is easy and safe from a lost laptop, fire, flood, or theft. If you run a NAS at home, pCloud supports backing it up via WebDAV, Rsync, SFTP, and SCP, making it a real offsite destination for a Synology NAS, not just a simple sync folder. It would be a perfect offsite backup for small businesses, remote workers, etc.

iCloud Photos is great, but it uses storage from your iCloud storage quota, which can get expensive as Apple’s cameras get better and better and file sizes keep increasing. Every pCloud plan includes pCloud Photos, a photo gallery that organizes everything by date on a timeline, automatically tags objects and scenes, and groups shots into albums by event and person.

The pCloud mobile app backs up your camera roll automatically to free up space on your iPhone; a Memories feature resurfaces older photos, as the Photos app does; and a built-in document scanner turns receipts and paperwork into PDFs without needing a separate app. Inside the app, there is also a built-in Photo Editor with crop, rotate, brightness, contrast, highlights, shadows, and eight one-click filters, so quick fixes don’t require moving it back to Apple Photos.

pCloud Docs covers documents, spreadsheets, presentations, PDFs, text, and markdown with six built-in editors and real-time collaboration, all from the browser or the mobile app. If your household is split, with one person on Microsoft, Apple, or Google, pCloud can pull in files from Google Photos, Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, and Facebook. That’s the easiest way I’ve seen to get everyone’s files into one place without needing to download and reupload everything.

Files and photos aren’t the only benefit of joining the pCloud ecosystem. pCloud Pass is a password manager that works across all devices, browsers, and operating systems, with one-click login, form filling, and a generator for strong, unique passwords. Passwords are still hard, and most people are either paying monthly for a manager or reusing the same three passwords. A lifetime license solves the annoying aspects of using a dedicated password manager app or being locked into Apple’s or Google’s systems.

pCloud Encryption is client-side, zero-knowledge encryption for your most sensitive files. In plain language: files in your Crypto folder are encrypted on your Mac before they upload, and only you hold the key. pCloud can’t read them, and neither can anyone else. It’s the right place for tax returns, scans of your birth certificate, and anything else you’d rather not have sitting in a regular sync folder.

Here’s the deal you’ll want to pay the most attention to: pCloud offers an exclusive 3in1 Bundle, because it knocks out two more subscriptions at once. It’s 3 TB of Lifetime storage plus Lifetime pCloud Pass and Lifetime pCloud Encryption, and it’s the only offer that includes everything you need to ditch a vast majority of your subscriptions. Count up what this level of storage and functionality would cost you over three or four years, and you’ll see how incredible of a deal it is. If you don’t sign up today, you’ll end up regretting it in 2030.

pCloud’s Black Friday pricing runs from November 13 through November 28. Every plan is a one-time payment with Lifetime access, no subscription, and no renewal.

You also get to choose where your data is stored, with data centers in Luxembourg and the United States, and everything is protected in transit with TLS/SSL. With pCloud, it’s your files and your rules, and one Lifetime deal protects everything.

If you’re tired of paying for storage every month, this is the week to stop. Grab pCloud’s Black Friday Lifetime deal before it ends on November 28.

The best time to sign up for pCloud’s lifetime deal was 9 years ago. The second best is today.

#3161. These 4 Travel Stocks Depend on Holiday Spending

Hotels, a booking app, rented cabins, and cruise ships: Here's how each of these four travel stocks makes money when families leave home for the holidays.

Marriott (MAR -0.35%), Booking Holdings (BKNG -1.00%), Airbnb (ABNB +3.12%), Carnival (CCL -0.38%): four stocks, one very old habit. When families leave home for the holidays, someone has to provide them with a place to stay, whether it's a hotel room, a booking app, a rented cabin, or a cabin at sea.

Getting there costs more this year. Airline tickets have surged, especially around the holidays, and award tickets for Thanksgiving flights between big U.S. airports cost 32% more miles than last year, per CNBC.

People are still going. The real question is how each of these travel companies gets paid when they do.

Marriott International doesn't own most of its hotels. It collects fees from owners who use its brands, so fuller, pricier rooms mean bigger checks. In the third quarter, revenue per available room (RevPAR), a measure of how much each room earns, rose 6.5% worldwide and 7.4% in the U.S. and Canada. Management raised its full-year forecast and expects RevPAR to grow by 4.5% to 5% in the fourth quarter.

Vacationers did the heavy lifting. Leisure RevPAR rose 9% in the U.S. and Canada as people "continue to prioritize in-person experiences like travel," CEO Anthony Capuano said on the earnings call.

The holiday angle goes beyond rooms. Franchise and management fees rose 13%, helped by higher fees from Marriott Bonvoy co-branded credit cards. Bonvoy now has about 309 million members.

Booking Holdings, which owns a host of sites such as Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, Kayak, and OpenTable, had a strong summer. Room nights, meaning one room booked for one night, grew 7%, and gross bookings, the total value of trips sold, rose 10% to $54.5 billion.

But demand cooled late in the quarter, especially for international trips, and October brought new trouble from the Middle East conflict, higher airfares, and unrest in some European cities. Booking expects room nights to grow just 1% to 3% this quarter. The bright spot is close to home: Domestic travel "has remained resilient."

Investors have noticed the slowdown. Shares closed at $160 recently, after a 25-for-1 stock split in April, and they're down about 25% this year. If holiday sales hold up better than management fears they will, that's where the surprise could come from.

Airbnb is the one made for holiday gatherings, such as when a dozen relatives want a house with one big kitchen. Its third quarter showed real momentum: Nights and seats booked rose 16%, revenue grew 19% to $4.9 billion, and growth in first-time bookers sped up to 13%, the fastest since early 2022. Airbnb raised its full-year outlook and expects fourth-quarter revenue to climb 16% to 18%.

It's also making holiday trips easier to say yes to. Its "reserve now, pay later" lets guests lock in eligible stays without paying anything up front, which Airbnb pitches for family trips "where everyone's still sorting out who owes what." Searches for Christmas-to-New Year's stays are jumping in small mountain towns a few hours' drive from big cities. For example, they're up 37% for Hunter, New York, in the Catskills.

Carnival works differently. People book cruises months ahead and put down deposits, so the company knows a lot about its holiday season before it arrives. Customer deposits hit a third-quarter record of $7.6 billion, up about 7%, even though it isn't adding capacity over the next 12 months, and 2027 bookings are at record occupancy and prices.

About half of Carnival's sailings in its fiscal first quarter, which runs December through February, head to the Caribbean. Its private island stops help, too. Celebration Key in the Bahamas welcomed almost 2.5 million guests in its first year.

Fuel prices are the catch. Higher fuel prices knocked about $150 million off this year's profit outlook since June, though better pricing and efficiency more than made up for it. Of these four companies, Carnival's the one whose holiday money is already in the bank.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We’re halfway through November now, and I know I need some good movies to help distract me from the biting cold. Luckily, Prime Video has stocked up its increasingly compulsive library in impressive style this month. To stop you from scrolling for ages until you land on a film you fancy, I’ve handpicked three flicks I think you’ll have a grand old time with this weekend on one of the best streaming services.

First, a classic drama deservedly picked up a couple of Oscars back in 1998, and for me it features the late, great Robin Williams' second best role (after "Aladdin's" Genie, naturally). Then there's a thoroughly stupid but lovable comedy that showed the world Arnie could do lolz. Finally, I’ve chosen a sci-fi thriller that gave Matthew Broderick one of his first starring roles.

So wrap up warm, break out some junk food and read on for three movies you should definitely stream on Prime Video this weekend.

“How do you like them apples?” I like them mighty fine, Mr. Hunting. The movie that finally won Robin Williams a richly deserved Oscar for Best Supporting Actor, “Good Will Hunting” was a passion project both Matt Damon and Ben Affleck had been working on for years before they got a Hollywood studio to bite. Damon plays the titular Will Hunting; a tough Southie kid from Boston who just so happens to be a secret mathematical genius.

His absurdly high IQ is discovered by Professor Geral Lambeau (Stellan Skarsgård) who catches Will solving an insanely challenging math problem on a chalkboard as Hunting is half-assing a shift as a janitor at MIT. Lambeau promptly takes Will under his wing, but it’s clear that this genius needs help. Abused from an early age and carrying a lot of rage, it’s Williams’ Dr Sean Maguire who helps Hunting find some peace.

There’s also an utterly charming romance between Will and fellow student Skylar (a lovely Minnie Driver) that drives much of the movie. The only thing that ticks me off about this classic is that we never got “Good Will Hunting 2: Hunting Season” that “Jay and Silent Bob Strike Back” promised me in 2001.

Watch "Good Will Hunting" on Prime Video now

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

The first movie to really show off Arnie’s comedic chops. Although if you can’t have a giggle during “Predator’s” “stick around line” the year before this delightful comedy came out, I feel sorry for you. The premise of “Twins” is pretty ingenious. Thanks to a secret genetic experiment, hulking Julius Benedict (Schwarzenegger) and impish Vincent Benedict (Danny DeVito) are fraternal twins who are separated at birth.

Years later, Arnie’s hyper-smart, kind-hearted giant (he was raised by a professor on an isolated island) eventually tracks down DeVito, who has slipped into a life of crime and become a semi-sleazy crook. Once Vinnie finds himself pursued by mobsters after accidentally pilfering the prototype of a super-secret jet engine (no, really), the pair embark on a cross-country road trip that eventually reunites them with their mother, who thought they had both died at birth. “Twins” is a big-hearted ‘80s classic… though I do partially blame its existence on helping to birth 1994’s awful “Junior”.

“Shall we play a game?” Sure, why not? Oh, I’ve accidentally started the beginnings of a global thermonuclear war because I’m a high school hacker who thought it was clever to mess around with a military supercomputer. Oops. That sounds like a slightly mean synopsis of “WarGames” — a movie that I actually really like — but there’s no denying the basic plot is highly silly.

Still, Matthew Broderick shines in one of his first big breaks. Long before he was Ferris Bueller and legendarily bunked off for the day and a decade prior to him becoming King of Pride Rock, here he plays hacker and video game enthusiast David Lightman. Messing with an ultra-brainy computer, then accidentally entering its WOPR (War Operation Plan Response) quickly causes a national crisis. David basically thinks he’s playing Battleship, while over at the Pentagon, they’re in full-on DEFCON 5 mode as military brass try to stave off World War III with the Russians. It’s silly, it’s sweet, and I wholeheartedly recommend streaming “WarGames” this weekend.

Dave was a computing editor at Tom’s Guide who covered everything from cutting edge laptops to ultrawide monitors. Now he contributes to the site in a freelance capacity. When he’s not worrying about dead pixels, Dave enjoys regularly rebuilding his PC for absolutely no reason at all. In a previous life, he worked as a video game journalist for 15 years, with bylines across GamesRadar+, PC Gamer and TechRadar. Despite owning a graphics card that costs roughly the same as your average used car, he still enjoys gaming on the go and is regularly glued to his Switch. Away from tech, most of Dave’s time is taken up by walking his husky, buying new TVs at an embarrassing rate and obsessing over his beloved Arsenal.

#3159. Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep an eye on things – even upstairs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Home Security

Alongside the Ring Drone Cam, Ring introduced the Rover Cam for businesses. It investigates disturbances and streams 4K footage.

Today, Ring announced the launch of a new subbrand, Ring Robotics, with two new products: the $249 Ring Drone Cam, an indoor “mobile security camera” drone that shoots 2K video, and the $999 Ring Rover Cam, a security robot for businesses that patrols autonomously and investigates disturbances.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Studio gives Alexa+ an AI camera to see inside your home

Both devices use Ring’s custom navigation software, “AI Pilot,” to autonomously navigate interior spaces and move between set points along a patrol, rather than being controlled directly by the user. AI Pilot leverages the devices’ cameras, sensors, and vision models, along with cloud processing, to create interior maps, then move the devices between predesignated patrol points such as a side door or a window.

I recently saw both new robots in person at a showcase in New York hosted by Ring’s founder and chief inventor, Jamie Siminoff. They certainly do what they advertise but come with some significant limitations. The drone, for example, can only stay in the air for about 8 minutes before it needs to dock and recharge, while the Ring Rover Cam is slow and deliberate, seemingly ideal for routine surveillance rather than rapid response to an event.

The Ring Drone Cam moves around predetermined patrol points in your home, sending you a live 2K video feed whether you’re just in another room or out of town. The user doesn’t actually fly the drone; instead, it moves around autonomously using Ring’s custom “AI Pilot” navigation technology, leveraging its cameras, sensors, and cloud processing to create a map of its surroundings. This allows it to fly through the air at an appropriate height, going from room to room, even up stairs.

In the Ring app, the user creates patrol points they want the drone to move between — likely a window, doorway, or high-traffic room — creating a set path that is both predictable (so you always know where the drone will go) and relevant, so it’s only monitoring the areas you want it to. But here is where its limitations come into play: It needs a finite path to navigate because its flight time is limited to just five to eight minutes in the air before it has to return to its charging dock.

That makes the dock both the start and end point for the drone’s routine trips, and it’s designed with this in mind. When it goes to land, the drone hovers over the dock and lowers itself down, dropping into place so it can start charging automatically. I asked about its potential to land elsewhere, and Ring told me it would only make an emergency landing outside of its dock in case it didn’t have enough power to get home.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Dot can turn into a Wi-Fi extender – how it works

There’s one other very important caveat: This thing is loud. There’s no sneaking up on anyone with the Ring Drone Cam, as the entire household is likely to hear it the second it undocks. The four propellers emit a constant, high-pitched whirring while in the air that’s loud enough to announce its presence to anyone in the vicinity: intruder or resident.

During the product briefing, Siminoff insinuated that this was part of its design to dissuade home intruders snooping around your house at night (especially when paired with the drone’s front-facing spotlight), but it’s likely just the result of its engineering, especially considering this is a first-gen product. It’s so loud that it makes me think it’s better suited to navigating the home when no one’s home (although whether or not your pets go bonkers trying to catch it is a whole other issue).

The Ring Drone is designed to work out of the box with the existing Ring ecosystem, including the 2K Video Doorbell and Indoor Cam, and is also compatible with Amazon’s Map View.

The Ring Drone Cam will start shipping on Jan. 27, 2027, and will cost $249.

The other product Ring announced is the Rover Cam, a mobile robot with a 4K camera designed to monitor large spaces like warehouses, offices, or businesses. Ring calls it a “security guard that never clocks out,” but it’s more like a slow-moving droid that goes on set patrol paths. It leverages the same AI Pilot technology as the Ring Drone to map its surroundings and navigate around shelving, furniture, and obstacles in real time.

It’s much quieter than its airborne sibling, traveling at low speeds and offering mobile surveillance instead of wiring every square inch of a large space. If the technology here looks familiar, it’s because it resembles the Amazon Astra, a smaller robot designed for home monitoring but with a very similar build.

The idea here is to deploy the robot to certain areas of a workplace via the app, then get 360-degree views once it’s there. Like the drone, it can also set out on automated routes at select timing intervals — like right after a business closes or before it opens. During working hours, it chugs along with its camera, capturing everything in its view.

Also: The 4 biggest Amazon smart home announcements from today

If another Ring device is triggered, the Rover Cam autonomously goes to investigate the disturbance, providing 4K footage in real time via the app. It also features a periscope camera that can extend to see over obstacles like shelving, counters, or furniture, providing a high-level view if needed. In case you lose it in a large warehouse or office, it has a “light tower” that projects light upward onto the ceiling, notifying users of its location.

Even when docked, it uses motion-sensing technology to start recording the second it senses any kind of movement, just like Ring doorbell cameras. In case of an emergency, the Rover features a siren and red flashing lights to dissuade intruders.

The Ring Rover Cam is available for preorder now and will start shipping on Dec. 16, 2026. It will cost $999.

#3158. 5 apps I need Siri AI to work with now that it’s open to third-party developers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Smart Assistants

With the latest betas for iOS and other platforms, Siri AI is now available to all developers for full integration into their apps. Here are the ones I hope will jump on board.

One of the many benefits of the new Siri AI is its ability to work directly with apps on your device via a feature known as App Intents. Currently, this skill includes many of Apple’s own built-in apps and some third-party ones. But with the latest public and developer betas for iOS 27.3, the company is expanding support to all third-party developers.

Also: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade

With App Intents, you’re able to ask Siri to tackle a variety of actions among various built-in and third-party apps. On a basic level, you can tell it to perform tasks such as getting directions, playing music, scheduling meetings, sending messages, adding reminders, and finding photos.

On a more advanced level, you can ask it to do things like organize your inbox, edit a photo, and analyze and help you with your current screen. You could also tell it to combine several actions in one shot, work across multiple apps, and engage in a natural back-and-forth conversation.

Introduced in 2022 with iOS 16, the App Intents skill does play well with classic Siri, no Apple Intelligence required. This applies not just to built-in apps but also to third-party apps. However, classic Siri lacks the AI smarts and advanced skills of the latest version.

Siri AI fully supports most built-in apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It does support some third-party apps, but its more advanced features are limited or unavailable.

That’s the gap the new developer betas aim to close. With iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, MacOS 27.3, and VisionOS 27.3, all developers will be able to use Siri AI to fully support and integrate with their apps. For example, instead of manually opening an app like DoorDash or Grubhub to check or change a food order, you can tell Siri to do it for you.

Also: The Siri AI waitlist is gone in iOS 27: How to try the beta now

“Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, on-screen awareness, natural language, and more,” Apple said in a news release for developers. “So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.”

As I use many third-party apps on my iPhone and iPad, both personally and professionally, I’m looking forward to enhanced support for the ones I rely on. With that in mind, here are five apps for which I’d welcome the new and full Siri AI integration.

I often use Amazon on my iPhone and iPad to shop for and purchase items, review my wishlist, and check the status of products I’ve ordered. To do any of those things, I have to open the app and manually go to the right screens. How convenient it would be if I could tell Siri to handle those tasks for me.

“Siri, search for the 512GB 2026 iPad mini on Amazon and add it to my shopping cart.”

“Siri, review my Amazon wishlist for the luggage I recently added and tell me the latest prices.”

“Siri, check the delivery status of the Alexa photo frame I just ordered on Amazon.”

Right now, Siri can’t do any of those things. But if Siri AI and App intents are fully integrated with Amazon, I may just be able to accomplish those tasks in the future.

IMDB is my go-to app for getting info on movies, TV shows, performers, directors, and more. After I open the app and run a search, I often want specific details, such as the rating and runtime of a particular film or TV episode.

Also: AI completely changed how I develop iPhone apps

To simplify that process, I’ve love to be able to ask Siri: “Siri, search IMDB for the 1935 movie ‘The Bride of Frankenstein,’ give me the running time, tell me where I can stream it, and add it to my watchlist.” If Siri could accomplish all that at some point, it would get a round of applause from me.

I borrow and read a lot of e-books through my local library systems, and I use the handy Libby app for that. Here, I can search different libraries for books by title, author, or subject. I can then borrow a book and read it through the Libby app or, more typically, through the Amazon Kindle app. For this, I have to manually open the app and search among the various libraries for the book I want.

Also: I lost 100 pounds in 7 months: How a smart scale and Apple Watch helped

Instead, I’d like to ask Siri to do that for me. I might say: “Siri, look in Libby for books about Alan Turing, give me the titles of the ones you find, and tell me which ones are currently available to borrow.”

My wife and I are big theater buffs, and we see a lot of plays on Broadway when we’re in New York and on the West End when we’re in London. Often, I buy tickets through the TodayTix service and app. For this, I’ll open the app, set the location to New York or London, look for a specific play, and then try to find seats for a certain day and time.

If TodayTix is ever fully supported by Siri AI and App Intents, I might be able to ask Siri to track down the right seats for me. I could say: “Siri, look for the play ‘Rent’ in London, give me the available performances for Dec. 5 through 9, and let me know which seats are accessible in the first 10 rows.”

As my wife and I often travel and dine out, Yelp is another app I frequently use. Here, I also have to manually launch the app and run searches for restaurants and other places. I then have to try to filter or sort the results based on location, price, and ratings.

Also: 3 handy iPhone features that make my life easier – even doing laundry

Asking Siri to tackle those tasks would certainly be a time saver. I could ask it to “find the closest Italian restaurants using Yelp and show me ones within a one-mile radius that have earned four stars or higher.”

With App Intents, Siri AI can already handle advanced, complex, multi-step tasks for built-in apps. With all developers now able to take advantage of this same support, I’m expecting a lot of apps to jump on board. Let’s hope my favorites end up on the list.

#3157. Is Your Console Ready for Grand Theft Auto 6? Here’s What You Can Do to Make Room

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Deleting old games isn’t the only option you have to make space for GTA 6.

Grand Theft Auto 6 hits shelves on Nov. 19, 2026, and if you preordered the game, you can preload it on your PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X/S now. Preloading ensures you can quickly boot the game up when it’s released.

Rockstar Games revealed that GTA 6 is 212 GB, which will take up about half of my Xbox Series S’s storage space. The company announced that GTA 6 is available to stream via Xbox Cloud Gaming without downloading it to your console. However, cloud streaming GTA 6 might affect the game’s performance and relies heavily on a strong internet connection. To avoid those issues, I plan on downloading the game.

If you’re like me and are excited to play GTA 6 but don’t have much storage space, you have two options: delete games or upgrade your console’s hard drive. Here’s what you should know about both options.

The simplest and cheapest way to free up space on your console for Grand Theft Auto 6 is to delete files and other games, which is what I’ll be doing. Uninstalling games is a good choice for folks who plan on spending a lot of time with GTA 6 and don’t intend to juggle different games. Rob Nelson, who oversees Rockstar North with Aaron Garbut, told The New York Times that he had an 80-hour playthrough of the game in February, so you can easily stay immersed in Grand Theft Auto’s state of Leonida.

You may not need to delete much – uninstalling a game like Call of Duty alone could free up nearly 315 GB, giving you enough digital storage for GTA 6. Since deleting files is almost instantaneous, you can quickly reclaim hard drive space. Because you don’t need to buy additional storage, you’ll also save a lot of money – storage prices are through the roof at the moment.

Ultimately, deleting games is a great option if you don’t want to spend any additional money or you don’t mind redownloading games later.

If you plan on hopping between GTA 6 and other games, or you don’t want to delete many of your downloaded titles, you can upgrade your console’s storage. Buying storage is more expensive than deleting files from your console, but benefit from being able to seamlessly hop between Grand Theft Auto 6 and Call of Duty or Madden.

You can use internal or external storage for your console, but you might have to move files between your internal and external storage to launch games. An internal hard drive lets you seamlessly play games. Xbox consoles rely on proprietary expansion cards from Seagate or SanDisk that plug into your console for additional storage. The PlayStation 5 uses M.2 solid-state drives, which are installed alongside the PS5’s built-in storage, and CNET’s David Carnoy recommends the Lexar NM 790 as a fast SSD with a straightforward installation process.

There shouldn’t be any performance, quality or load-time differences between running games from installed storage expansion devices versus your console’s internal storage. Both expansion cards and SSDs can be expensive, especially when compared with deleting games.

You could also use an external hard drive to expand your storage, which can be cheaper than buying expansion cards and internal SSD upgrades – you may even have a compatible USB external drive sitting around that you can use. However, there are caveats around what games can and can’t be played directly from external HDDs.

For Xbox consoles, some older Xbox, Xbox 360 and Xbox One titles can be stored and played from external HDDs. But games optimized for Series X/S consoles can only be stored on HDDs and must be moved back to your internal drive to play. Similarly, the PlayStation 5 only lets you store PS5 games on external HDDs, while you can store and run PS4 games from external drives.

Therefore, using an external HDD requires playing digital musical chairs, moving current-gen games back and forth between your external hard drive and internal console storage in order to play them. The LaCie Rugged SSD4 earned a CNET Editors’ Choice Award and could be a good option. If its price tag scares you, the Western Digital P10 offers more storage at a more economical price point.

Rockstar announced that GTA 6 will be available to stream on the Xbox consoles – no download required – via Xbox Cloud Gaming, with some quality and time limitations. You’ll need to purchase either an Xbox Game Pass plan or Cloud Gaming hours. Folks who don’t want to delete games or upgrade their console storage can stream GTA 6, but you’ll need an Xbox One or Series X/S console, won’t get the highest visual quality and will have to pay for more playtime hours if they run out. Streaming GTA 6 could help budget-conscious gamers who don’t want to upgrade from Xbox One consoles or who don’t have the allotted storage space on their devices.

Normally, you can stream many games on PCs, mobile devices and TVs or streaming devices using Xbox Cloud Gaming or Game Pass, but Grand Theft Auto 6 is limited to the Xbox One, Series S and Series X. Additionally, GTA 6 streaming quality is capped at Series S graphical settings. So if you have a Series X, consider deleting games or upgrading your storage to run the game locally with better graphics.

While you’ll need to install the full game on your console first, remote play for Xbox and PlayStation consoles lets you stream GTA 6 to other devices, like your phone, tablet, streaming device or TV.

If you’re willing to pay a little more for the convenience of having multiple games ready to play at a moment’s notice, Xbox expansion cards or an internal SSD for a PS5 are your best options. If you want a cheaper option and don’t mind moving game files around, an external hard drive could be for you. If you have Xbox Game Pass or Xbox Cloud Gaming, you could stream the game to your console without needing more storage space. However, the cheapest option is to delete games from your internal storage and redownload them later, which can be time-consuming.

You only have a few days left until Rockstar releases GTA 6, so you’d better prepare your digital storage now, or you might not be immediately able to play. I plan on deleting old games to make room on my console. You won’t catch me slipping on Nov. 19.

#3156. Better Chip Stock: Nvidia vs. AMD

The things affecting Nvidia's stock price are not entirely related to the state of its business.

Nvidia (NVDA -2.01%) shareholders have had a rough few days. After a week in which news broke that CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang had engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman who is accused of being a Chinese spy, and another with an Nvidia executive, on Thursday morning, he resigned.

The exit of the man who has been the face of the company for decades has investors worried about its future. AMD (AMD -8.75%) shareholders aren't in the same boat, and the chipmaker is enjoying surging data center sales.

However, the question remains: Which stock is the better buy? It's a hard question to answer, because at face value, Nvidia is doing far better than AMD. But AMD doesn't have other questions surrounding the state of its business.

What matters is what you value most as an investor, as Nvidia is likely to be a tumultuous stock to own over the next few months.

Before comparing Nvidia and AMD stocks, investors must answer a different question: How capable will Nvidia be without Huang in the CEO role? If you’re of the view that the company’s future really rests on the caliber of the person in the top job, then Nvidia’s investment thesis can’t be properly analyzed until his permanent successor is picked. For now, respected CFO Colette Kress occupies the role on an interim basis.

If it doesn't matter to you who is leading Nvidia, then you're free to proceed to the next point.

Nvidia and AMD are both computing unit designers, although their businesses look a bit different. AMD's product lineup is a lot broader than Nvidia's, and so is its customer base. It has sizable businesses in the consumer electronics world as well as in embedded processors and data centers. However, almost all investors care about is the data center business, as that's what is growing rapidly right now.

During Q3, AMD's data center revenue rose 97% year over year to $8.5 billion. That's a strong result, and investors are excited. However, because AMD also has fairly large exposure to other segments, its overall growth rate was 45%, bringing its top line to $13.4 billion. The problem is it isn't anywhere close to Nvidia's growth and size.

Nvidia reports its fiscal 2027 Q3 results on Nov. 17. But until we get that update about the recent state of the business, the best we can do is to use its fiscal Q2 results. In that period, its data center sales rose 117% year over year to $89 billion. Because Nvidia's data center business makes up a far larger chunk of its total, Nvidia's overall revenue growth rate was 106% to $96.2 billion.

Nothing that has transpired over the past week will affect what Nvidia reports in Q3, and I'd expect another quarter of outperforming AMD based on historical trends. Furthermore, Nvidia has already told investors to expect 70% revenue growth in its fiscal 2028. Management is comfortable giving that guidance because Nvidia's business is practically locked in, with AI hyperscalers ordering its processors far in advance of when they'll be ready to install them in data centers.

I think this supports the premise that Nvidia can keep succeeding without Huang as CEO, because it's already got a lot of future growth on the books due to how strong a business it has built.

So, from a growth standpoint, Nvidia is still the better pick. And after this month’s sell-off, the stock is even cheaper.

The best way to weigh the value of these two stocks is to look at their expected earnings for next year. By that metric, AMD is about 3 times more expensive than Nvidia.

NVDA PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

That seems like a huge premium to pay for AMD, and the reality is that regardless of who is running Nvidia, a pricing mismatch of that magnitude is too great to ignore. Nvidia's stock could triple from this point without looking too expensive, and even a double would leave the stock looking cheap compared to its growth rate.

I think Nvidia is the far better stock to buy here, mainly due to how cheap the stock is. Nvidia's business is strong, and its board should find a talented new leader to take it over.
